family.name: Performance Marketing
family.summary: A D2C brand with a budget cut, over-claiming ad dashboards and an agency plan with flaws that only show up if you do the unit economics.

stages.title: Warm-up
stages.summary: A 45-second spontaneous answer. Not scored; gives a voice sample to compare with later recordings.

stages.title: First read
stages.summary: Read the channel table and say what worries them most. Think aloud: shows whether they spot over-attribution and unit economics.

stages.title: The budget cut
stages.summary: Commit to where a budget cut comes from and estimate the impact on orders. Think aloud.

stages.title: Two weeks later
stages.summary: The situation changes based on their cut. Tests whether they update on new data and explain why it happened.

stages.title: Critique the agency's plan
stages.summary: Critique an agency plan with planted flaws, including a target ROAS below break-even. Think aloud.

stages.title: Founder update (AI allowed)
stages.summary: Write a founder update with any AI tool and paste the conversation. Shows how they work with AI, not just whether they use it.

stages.title: A real decision
stages.summary: A real budget or channel decision from their career that didn't go to plan. Checks specificity and ownership.

brief.text: You've just joined **Pawprint Pantry** as its first in-house performance marketer. Pawprint Pantry is a D2C pet food brand selling fresh-cooked dog food online. The founder runs the business day to day, and an agency, Growthline Media, runs paid media.

brief.caption: Last month, as reported by each ad platform

brief.text: Same month, from the store backend

items: Average order value: **₹899**
Gross margin after product, shipping and payment costs: **45%**
About 31% of customers order again within 90 days.

brief.text: The company and numbers are fictional, and every candidate gets a slightly different version. A calculator is fine.

prompt.text: What is one marketing metric you think people rely on too much, and why?
Keep it under 45 seconds. This one is not scored; it just gets you talking.

reviewerGuide.text: Not scored. On the verification call, listen for the same voice and ask a related question to check it is the same person.

prompt.text: It's your first morning at Pawprint Pantry. Looking at last month's numbers, **what worries you most, and what is the first number you would check before changing anything?**
Refer to specific figures. One sharp point beats a list of ten.

reviewerGuide.text: Strong answers notice at least one of these:

items: **Over-attribution.** Dashboards claim 7,714 orders, but the store recorded 6,042, so platforms over-claim by about 28%. Channel ROAS can't be taken at face value.

**Unit economics.** Blended CPA is ₹364 against a first-order break-even CPA of ₹405 (AOV × margin). The business is only just profitable on first orders, and repeat purchase (31%) has to carry the rest.
**Retargeting and brand search look too good.** 7.1x reported ROAS on retargeting mostly reflects people who were already going to buy.

reviewerGuide.text: Weak answers give generic advice ("refresh creatives", "optimise targeting") without touching the numbers, or take platform ROAS literally and pour budget into retargeting.

rubric.label: Works from the actual numbers
anchors: No specific figures; generic advice.
Quotes figures but does not connect them.
Connects two or more figures into a conclusion (e.g. CPA vs break-even).
Spots a non-obvious relationship, such as over-attribution, and quantifies it.

rubric.label: Measurement scepticism
anchors: Takes platform ROAS at face value.
Mentions attribution vaguely.
Says which channel numbers are least trustworthy and why.
Proposes a concrete check sized to this business (holdout, geo split, post-purchase survey, code/UTM audit).

rubric.label: Prioritisation
anchors: A list of everything.
Several priorities, unclear order.
One clear priority with a reason.
Clear priority plus what would change their mind.

choices.label: Spread the cut evenly across channels

prompt.text: The founder has cut next month's paid media budget by **25%**, to **₹16,50,000**, and wants orders to stay roughly flat. Retargeting is small; leave it out of this decision.
**Where does most of the cut come from?** Pick one, then explain:

items: why this channel,
what you expect to happen to store orders next month (give a number and how you got it),
the risk you are accepting, and the early warning you would watch.

reviewerGuide.text: There is no single right answer. Good answers commit, estimate the order impact from marginal (not average) CPA, recognise that cutting prospecting starves retargeting and brand search later, and name an early-warning metric.
"Spread evenly" can be fine if it comes with a stated test plan; it is weak when it avoids the decision.

rubric.label: Commits and reasons from unit economics
anchors: No clear choice, or reasoning is generic.
Makes a choice with a plausible but unquantified reason.
Reasons from CPA, margin or attribution quality specific to this scenario.
Reasons about marginal returns and second-order effects between channels.

rubric.label: Quantified expectation
anchors: No estimate.
A number with no logic behind it.
A number with a clear, if simple, method.
A range with assumptions stated and a sense of confidence.

rubric.label: Risk and monitoring
anchors: Risk not mentioned.
Generic risk ("orders may drop").
Specific risk tied to the channel chosen.
Specific risk plus a metric, threshold and timing for reacting.

prompt.text: Two weeks in, Meta-reported orders are down 40%, roughly as you planned. But Google Search orders are also down 15%, mostly on searches for "Pawprint Pantry", and your retargeting audiences have shrunk by about a third.
The founder asks: **"Was cutting Meta a mistake?"** What do you tell them, and what do you do this week?

reviewerGuide.text: They chose **Meta prospecting** in the previous question.

Tests whether they understand that prospecting feeds brand search and retargeting pools (the halo). Strong: explains the mechanism, proposes a partial restore or a structured test, and quantifies it. Weak: blames seasonality or defends the plan without looking at the new data.

prompt.text: Two weeks in, a competitor has started bidding on "Pawprint Pantry" as a keyword. Your brand CPC is up 60% and the competitor now appears above you for your own name on 54% of searches.
You cut Search. **What do you do this week, and what do you tell the founder?**

reviewerGuide.text: They chose **Google Search** in the previous question.

Tests brand defence. Strong: restores brand-term bidding quickly (cheap, high-intent), keeps any generic cut, considers a trademark complaint, and plans to measure how incremental brand search really is. Weak: ignores it, or restores all of Search.

prompt.text: Two weeks in, a creator you paid last month posts about Pawprint Pantry without being paid. Over three days you get about 109 extra orders, almost all tagged "Direct / none" in analytics, and nobody uses a discount code.
The founder says: **"Influencers work when we don't pay them. Cancel all the contracts."** What do you tell them?

reviewerGuide.text: They chose **Influencers** in the previous question.

Tests attribution literacy. Strong: explains that codes under-count influencer impact, that the unpaid post may be a result of the past paid relationship, warns against generalising from one event, and proposes better measurement (unique links, "how did you hear about us?" survey). Weak: agrees with the founder.

variants.label: If they chose "Spread the cut evenly across channels"

prompt.text: Two weeks in, every channel is down roughly in proportion and store orders are down 35%, worse than the 25% cut would suggest.
The founder says: **"You didn't make a decision, you made a spreadsheet."** What do you change now?

reviewerGuide.text: They chose **Spread the cut evenly across channels** in the previous question.

Tests whether they can admit the weakness and adapt. Strong: explains why even cuts hurt (campaigns fall below learning thresholds, fixed creative and agency costs), consolidates into the best marginal channels, and sets a clear test. Weak: defensive, or swings to an unreasoned all-in bet.

rubric.label: Updates on new information
anchors: Ignores or dismisses the new data.
Acknowledges it but keeps the plan unchanged without a reason.
Separates what the data shows from what it only suggests, and adjusts.
Adjusts in proportion to the evidence and says what would trigger a bigger change.

rubric.label: Explains the mechanism
anchors: No explanation of why it happened.
A plausible but generic explanation.
A correct mechanism specific to the channel.
A correct mechanism plus how to prove it.

rubric.label: Concrete next step this week
anchors: No action.
Vague action ("monitor closely").
A specific action with an owner or timing.
A specific action, the expected result and how the founder will know.

prompt.text: Growthline Media has sent their plan for next month (budget ₹16,50,000). **Pick the three problems that matter most for Pawprint Pantry right now, in order.** For each, say why it is a problem using the numbers, and what you would do instead.
You do not need to comment on every item.

reviewerGuide.text: Planted problems, roughly in order of how much they reveal:

items: **#2 Target ROAS is below break-even.** At 45% margin, first-order break-even ROAS is 2.22x, so a 1.8x target loses money on every attributed order, and more once you allow for platform over-claiming. The strongest expertise signal: generic AI critiques miss it unless given the margin.
**#3 Summing platform ROAS double-counts.** Dashboards over-claim by about 28% against store orders. Judge on blended CPA or MER against store orders.
**#5 The discount destroys margin.** A 20% discount cuts gross profit per order by about 44% (20% ÷ 45%), and the goal is flat volume, not growth.
**#1 Awareness spend won't pay back next month**, while the budget is being cut and orders must hold.

reviewerGuide.text: #4 is reasonable. Ranking it as a top-three problem is a negative signal.

material.text: Growthline Media: plan for next month

items: Move 35% of the budget into a YouTube brand-awareness campaign to build the funnel for Q4.
Set Meta campaigns to a target ROAS of 1.8x, comfortably above the category benchmark.
Report success as the sum of platform-reported ROAS across channels, as in the current dashboard.
Refresh ad creatives every two weeks and test three new hooks per week.
Run a 20% sitewide discount in week one to protect volume.

rubric.label: Finds the context-bound flaws
anchors: Misses #2, #3 and #5.
Finds one of them without the numbers.
Finds two with supporting numbers.
Finds #2 with the break-even maths plus at least one more.

rubric.label: Ranks by impact
anchors: No ranking, or ranks #4 highly.
Ranking present but unexplained.
Sensible ranking with reasons.
Ranking tied explicitly to next month's goal and the budget cut.

rubric.label: Concrete alternatives
anchors: Criticism only.
Vague alternatives.
A specific alternative for each problem.
Specific alternatives with numbers (e.g. a target ROAS above break-even).

prompt.text: Use any AI tool you like for this one. We are assessing how you use it, not whether you do.
Write the WhatsApp message (about 150 words) you would send Pawprint Pantry's founder summarising your plan for next month and the one risk they should know about.

items: Paste your final message.
Paste your full AI conversation, or write "none".
In 2–3 lines, say what you kept, changed or rejected from the AI and why.

reviewerGuide.text: Read the transcript first. Did they give the AI the real numbers and constraints? Did they catch wrong numbers or generic filler? Is the final message short, specific and written for a founder?
A polished message whose numbers do not match Pawprint Pantry's scenario (budget ₹16,50,000, 6,042 orders last month) is a red flag. "None" for the transcript is fine if the message itself is strong.

rubric.label: Judgment with AI
anchors: Pasted output unchanged, errors kept.
Light edits; did not give the AI the real context.
Gave the AI the context and fixed its mistakes.
Used AI deliberately (drafting, critique) and rejected weak suggestions with reasons.

rubric.label: Accurate to the scenario
anchors: Numbers wrong or invented.
Mostly generic; few scenario numbers.
Scenario numbers used correctly.
Numbers correct and consistent with their earlier answers.

rubric.label: Founder-ready communication
anchors: Long, vague or jargon-heavy.
Understandable but unfocused.
Clear plan and risk in plain language.
Could be sent as is; leads with the decision and the ask.

prompt.text: **Tell us about a real budget or channel decision you made that did not go to plan.** What were you looking at, what did you decide, what happened, and what would you do differently?
Specifics such as numbers and timelines matter more than polish.

reviewerGuide.text: Async answers here are easy to fabricate. Score specificity now, then verify on the call: rich detail that stays consistent under "why?" follow-ups is the signal. Stories that stay vague under follow-up questions are a warning sign.

rubric.label: Specificity
anchors: Hypothetical or generic.
A real situation, few specifics.
Concrete metrics, timeline and their own role.
Rich detail: what they saw, alternatives considered and what happened next.

rubric.label: Ownership and learning
anchors: Blames others or circumstances.
Takes some ownership; lesson is generic.
Clear ownership with a specific lesson.
Clear ownership, and shows how the lesson changed later decisions.
